items.q: What is the simplified acquisition threshold?
items.x: The reflex answer is $250,000 — a stale figure from outside the RFO, and the distractor every board reaches for. Get this one exact because it is load-bearing: the SAT gates simplified procedures and dozens of clause prescriptions, so an error here propagates into every one of them. $350,000, from 2.101, no qualifiers.

$10,000 is the reflex and it is wrong here — the RFO sets $15,000. Below the MPT the rules genuinely relax: awards may be made without soliciting competitive quotations when the price is reasonable, no written provisions or clauses are required, and the purchase card is a primary method. Get the ceiling wrong and you are either strangling small buys or waiving rules that still apply.

items.q: Who approves a J&A at or below $900,000?
items.x: At this tier the certification required by 6.104(a)(12) IS the approval — no separate signature chain above the contracting officer. The trap runs the other direction: assuming every sole source needs a higher blessing. Below $900,000 the KO who signs the justification owns it alone, which is why boards probe whether you treat that certification as a formality or as the whole safeguard.
d: The chief of the contracting office.
The head of the procuring activity.

items.q: Who approves a J&A above $900,000 up to $20M, and is it delegable?
items.a: The advocate for competition. Not delegable.
items.x: Half-credit trap: candidates name the advocate and drop 'not delegable.' Note the asymmetry — the next tier up, the head of the procuring activity, IS delegable to the general/flag-officer or above-GS-15 level, so non-delegability is specific to the advocate's tier, not a blanket rule. And officials at a higher level may always approve lower-dollar justifications; the table sets floors, not exclusive lanes.
d: The head of the procuring activity. Delegable to the flag-officer level.
The senior procurement executive. Not delegable.
The advocate for competition. Delegable in writing.
